title: Matthew 25:14–30
context: Jesus continues the readiness theme with a journeying master who entrusts unequal talents according to ability, then returns after a long time to settle accounts. Faithful servants enter the master’s joy; the fearful, idle servant loses even what he hid and is cast into outer darkness—stewardship under delayed return.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Matthew 25:14–30.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Our Lord proceeds by a parable still plainer (if that can be) to declare the final reward of a harmless man. May God give all such in this their day, ears to hear and hearts to understand it! The kingdom of heaven - That is, the King of heaven, Christ.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 25:14–30)

reformed.quote: By this term Christ does not distinguish between natural gifts and the gifts of the Spirit; for we have neither power nor skill which ought not to be acknowledged as having been received from God; and, therefore, whoever shall determine to give God his share will leave nothing for himself. What then is meant by saying, that the master of the house gives to each person more or less, according to his own ability?
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 25:14–30)

verses.text: “For it is like a man going into another country, who called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The kingdom is like a departing master entrusting property to servants—trust before absence.

Grace confers responsibility. What we hold is gift meant to be used, not merely admired.
verses.reformedNotes:
Journey, calling, entrustment: Christ frames discipleship as stewardship under His lordship.

Every talent is the Master’s property first. Assignment precedes accounting.

verses.text: To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts differ—five, two, one—each according to ability, then departure.

Unequal measures do not excuse unfaithfulness. Grace fits the trust to the servant and still expects faithful trading.
verses.reformedNotes:
Distribution is personal and measured. Ability is acknowledged; ownership remains the master’s.

God is not arbitrary in assignment, yet every servant remains accountable for what was given.

verses.text: Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents.
verses.arminianNotes:
Five-talent faithfulness acts at once and doubles the gift.

Grace energizes prompt obedience. Delay is not wisdom when the Master’s goods are in hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Immediate trading marks the faithful steward.

Effectual calling produces fruitful labor. The increase is still the master’s.

verses.text: In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two talents likewise produce two more—same faithfulness, smaller scale.

The standard is fidelity, not matching someone else’s five. Grace honors proportionate trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Equal commendation will meet unequal starting points when fidelity matches the trust.

God weighs faithfulness relative to entrustment, not envy of another’s sum.

verses.text: But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth and hid his lord’s money.
verses.arminianNotes:
One talent is buried—preservation without fruit, fear without faith.

Hiding gift can feel safe and still be disobedience. Grace calls the timid to risk obedience now.
verses.reformedNotes:
Burial looks careful and is rebellion against the purpose of the trust.

Sloth can wear the mask of caution. God sees the unused gift.

verses.text: “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
After a long time, settlement comes. Delay does not nullify audit.

Long absence tests motives. Live as those who will give account when He returns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Long time, then settling. The master’s calendar governs.

Delayed parousia is still certain judgment and reward.

verses.text: He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The five-talent servant reports increase with open hands.

Grace-grown fruit is gladly shown. Boasting is displaced by ‘you delivered… I have made.’
verses.reformedNotes:
Accounting begins with gift acknowledged and fruit presented.

Stewards confess both source and outcome under the master’s eye.

verses.text: “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Well done—faithful over little, set over much, enter the master’s joy.

The Master rewards fidelity without turning reward into wages that purchase salvation. Joy is shared life with Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Commendation, promotion, joy: the master’s verdict defines the servant’s future.

‘Well done’ is gracious speech to stewards kept faithful. Entrance into joy is gift and goal.
verses.keyContrast: Both treasure the master’s ‘Well done.’ Arminians emphasize rewarded faithfulness enabled by resistible grace; Reformed commentators often emphasize perseverance and reward as fruits of the master’s keeping grace.

verses.text: “He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The two-talent servant echoes the same confession and fruit.

Smaller trust, same gospel pattern—receive, trade, report.
verses.reformedNotes:
Parallel faithfulness under a smaller sum.

Reformed equality of praise will follow; the narrative already shows matching integrity.

verses.text: “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Identical ‘Well done’ and joy for the two-talent servant.

God is not impressed only by large portfolios. Faithful little is great in His joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master uses the same words and gives the same joy. The master’s pleasure tracks fidelity, not raw totals.

Unequal gifts, equal entrance into joy for the faithful.

verses.text: “He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter.
verses.arminianNotes:
The one-talent servant’s theology of the master is hard and extractive—reaping where he did not sow.

A distorted view of God breeds buried gifts. Grace invites a truer knowledge of the Master that frees obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Accusation against the master’s character precedes the excuse.

Bad theology of God licenses disobedience. The heart’s picture of the Lord shapes the hands.

verses.text: I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Fear hid the talent; ‘what is yours’ is returned unused.

Fear is understandable and still not faithfulness. Bring the gift into the open while bankers and fields remain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fear without faith produces burial, not stewardship.

Returning the unused gift does not equal obedience. God required increase fitting the trust.

verses.text: “But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wicked and slothful—the master names the heart and the inactivity.

The Master’s rebuke is meant to convert hearers before the settlement. Leave sloth; trust Him enough to trade.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wickedness and sloth are paired. Knowledge claimed (‘you knew’) becomes self-indictment.

The servant’s own words condemn him under the master’s justice.

verses.text: You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even bank interest would have been better than burial.

Minimal faithful risk beats pious inactivity. Grace stretches timid servants toward some obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master argues from the servant’s own premise: if I am hard, at least seek interest.

Excuses collapse. Some fruit was always required.

verses.text: Take away therefore the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents.
verses.arminianNotes:
Talent transferred to the one with ten—stewardship reallocated.

Unused trust can be reassigned. Hold gift loosely as the Master’s, urgently as your charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master redistributes for fruitfulness.

Gifts serve the master’s household, not the servant’s security blanket.

verses.text: For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abundance to the one who has; loss for the one who has not.

Living faith tends to grow; barren possession shrinks. Receive and trade while grace enables.
verses.reformedNotes:
Kingdom economy under the master: fruitful trust expands; empty hands lose even appearance.

God gives increase to living stewardship and removes unused forms.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject idle preservation as faithfulness. Arminians typically urge enabled, responsible trading now; Reformed interpreters press the master’s prerogative to give and take according to true fruit.

verses.text: Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Worthless servant cast into outer darkness—weeping and gnashing.

Arminian interpreters will not soften the end: this warning aims at repentance and faithful stewardship before that darkness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Outer darkness is the master’s verdict on worthless stewardship.

Jesus’ judgment language is serious. The warning magnifies the joy offered to faithful servants.
